title: Vayikra: the poor person's flour (Leviticus 2:1)
hook: for the flour offering the text says "soul"; Rashi: the poor person gives their very soul

segments.voice: Yesterday, korban: an offering that means coming near. Your line was offering means nearness. Today, the humblest offering in the book.

Chapter one of Leviticus is all animals: a bull from the herd, a sheep or a goat from the flock, or a bird, a turtledove or a young pigeon. Then chapter two opens with something much humbler. A bowl of fine flour, a little oil poured over it, a pinch of frankincense on top. The kind of thing anyone with a kitchen could bring. And the very first verse about this simple flour uses a word chapter one never used for the people bringing animals.
screen: `A BULL, A SHEEP, A BIRD.` → `THEN, A BOWL OF FLOUR.` → `A WORD CHAPTER ONE NEVER USED.`

segments.voice: The verse reads, "And when any one bringeth a meal-offering unto the LORD." But the Hebrew doesn't really say any one. It says nefesh: a soul. When a soul brings a meal offering. For the animals in chapter one, the text says adam, a person. Why does the flour get the soul? Rashi, drawing on the Talmud, answers: who usually brings a meal offering? The poor person, who can't afford an animal. And God says, as it were: I will count it as if he offered his very soul. In that reading, the less you have, the more of you is in what you give. A midrash makes it concrete. A woman brings a handful of flour to the Temple, and the priest looks down on it: what is there in this to eat, and what is there to offer? That night he dreams: don't despise her. It's as if she offered her soul. And the Mishnah, at the end of its tractate on meal offerings, gives a line still quoted today. Of the offerings of an animal, a bird and flour, it says: it's the same whether a person gives much or gives little, as long as they direct their heart to heaven. In the Mishnah's reading, the gifts aren't ranked by price.
screen: `FINE FLOUR, OIL, FRANKINCENSE.` · `NEFESH: A SOUL BRINGS IT.` · `DON'T DESPISE HER FLOUR.` · `MUCH OR LITTLE: THE SAME.` · then, large: `THE POOR BRING THEIR SOUL.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing you could give: a call to someone lonely, a note, ten minutes of real attention, a share of what's in your kitchen. Picture giving it with your whole attention, the way Rashi says the poor person's flour carries the giver's very soul. Let it be enough, exactly as it is.
Vayikra. And He called. The book where a bowl of flour brought by a poor person is described with the word for soul.
Your line: the poor bring their soul. A handful of flour can carry a whole person. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 382 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: VAYIKRA: SALT ON EVERY OFFERING.`

howItsDone: The Mishnah's teaching that much or little is the same, if the heart is directed to heaven, is often cited in Jewish teaching about charity and prayer.

chat.says: If someone can only afford a little flour, does their offering really count?
options: Yes. Leviticus calls the flour-giver a soul, and the Mishnah says much or little is the same.
Partly. Flour counted for less than an animal, so the poor had to bring it more often.
Only if the oil and frankincense on top together cost as much as a whole lamb would.
chat.meaning: Rashi says the poor person's flour counts as if they offered their soul; the Mishnah says much or little is the same, if the heart is directed to heaven.

nefesh.meaning: a soul; the word Leviticus 2:1 uses for the flour-giver

adam.meaning: a person; the word chapter one uses for those bringing animals

frankincense.meaning: a fragrant resin set on top of the flour offering

Rashi.meaning: a medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud

Mishnah.meaning: the early rabbis' collection of Jewish law and teaching

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook's 'if you can't afford those, a pair of birds' corrected (1:14 gives the bird offering without a means test; that is 5:7); 'a word not used for the animals' made precise (chapter one says adam); 'the Torah doesn't rank the gifts by price' reframed as the Mishnah's reading (5:7-11 does scale by means); cut 'one of the most precious words' and 'quoted ever since'; practice changed from recalling a received gift (too close to day 370) to giving one.
Leviticus 2:1 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm wording and hyphenation of 'meal-offering'.
Claim that the animal offerings use adam (a person) rather than nefesh: Leviticus 1:2 uses adam; confirm 'for the animal offerings' generalization.
Rashi on 2:1 / Menachot 104b; Leviticus Rabbah 3:5 (the woman's handful of flour and the priest's dream); Mishnah Menachot 13:11: confirm references.

The Torah does scale some offerings to a person's means (Leviticus 5:7–11); the myth line was reworded from 'the Torah ranks offerings by cost' to avoid overstating. Hook: birds as the option for those who can't afford herd or flock animals is from 1:14 and 5:7; confirm framing.
